item.title: Elon Musk on His Politics, a Potential Merger and Ukraine
item.description:
One of the biggest questions about Elon Musk is whether, with all of his businesses and wealth, he has too much influence.

The entrepreneur dominates satellite communications, which are vital in war zones, through his company SpaceX. He was one of the largest donors in the midterm elections, and he blasts his messages to 240 million followers on the social media platform X, which he owns.

At the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk in some ways downplayed his power.

He said that the Democratic victories in the midterms after his own record-setting donations to Republicans showed that money doesn’t have the power to buy elections; that shareholders would decide the fate of a potential SpaceX and Tesla merger (though Musk is the majority shareholder in both companies); and that only the part of his satellite communications business that’s run by the government could be used for offensive acts like drone strikes.

Musk also downplayed his once fervent support of President Trump, painting himself as a moderate: “I’m not MAGA,” he said. Here are five highlights from the conversation.

Musk gave nearly $500 million of campaign donations to support Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections — more than any person has ever spent in a cycle where they themselves were not a candidate.

At the DealBook Summit, in the wake of a Democratic landslide at the ballot box, he said that his effort had “failed”:

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it — or maybe it would have been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money.”

He added:

“If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

Musk was a fervent supporter of Trump during the run-up to the 2024 election, spending more than $250 million, making hundreds of social media posts and appearing at rallies. He not only once declared himself “MAGA,” but “dark, gothic MAGA.”

On Wednesday, Musk sought to reposition himself as a political moderate. First he said he was optimistic about Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic governor-elect of Texas, where many of his companies are based:

“I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor. And based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor.”

He also said that he thought it would be good for the parties to split political power:

“It’s good to have some balance of power, like not have, as a general rule, the presidency, Senate and House all be of the same party.”

And he sought to distance himself from Trump’s Make America Great Again movement:

“I’m not MAGA. Well, at least I’m not like, I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”

Musk said in October that Tesla and SpaceX, his two major businesses, were exploring a merger. He is the largest shareholder in both companies.

At the DealBook Summit, he boosted the idea, noting that both SpaceX and Tesla have major A.I. software groups:

“There’s more and more areas of interaction or overlap with SpaceX and Tesla that didn’t exist before.”

He also said it would be up to shareholders to decide whether a merger would happen:

“These require shareholder votes, which may or may not succeed, at least in the case of Tesla. But even for my shareholder vote for SpaceX, I have to represent other shareholders. I can’t just drag them into a noneconomic merger that is bad for them, because I’ll obviously get sued.”

Limits on Ukraine’s access to a satellite communications system run by SpaceX led drones to fall out of the sky on the front line in October, and have not been fully explained. The episode put a spotlight on Musk’s geopolitical influence.

At the DealBook Summit, Musk doubled down on his explanation that Ukraine had violated the rules for his civilian service, Starlink, which bans offensive uses like drone strikes. Starshield, a separate system, he said, could be used for such purposes, but is under the purview of the U.S. military:

“From the beginning, I’ve said that Starlink is a civilian system. It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people. If you want to do that, you need to do Starshield, which is, um, a separate system that is controlled by the U.S. government. But do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions.”

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has said the country’s access to Starshield has been restricted several times. Musk said that Zelensky was wrong to say Ukraine had always used Starshield: “He’s not always truthful.”

Musk defended Jensen Huang, the former Nvidia chief executive who was ousted after revelations he’d had a relationship with a woman identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset and another who was a subordinate. Musk’s companies rely on Nvidia chips.

“You need to think long and hard before kicking someone else like that out. I know that he’s certainly made some mistakes here. But I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States. I’ve been clear, I think it’s like taking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders. You have to balance the good that someone does and brings relative to the bad.”

Thanks for reading! We’ll see you tomorrow.
